title: Berkshire 1985 letter: textile exit, boat vs. rowing, option pitfalls, and buying Cap Cities and Scott Fetzer
summary: Buffett explains why size dampens returns, why shutting down the textile business taught that business quality beats managerial brilliance, and how fixed-price options reward retained earnings rather than performance. He also covers buying at a discount to business value, Washington Post and Cap Cities, insurance as a commodity, and Berkshire's acquisition criteria.

principles.text: A good managerial record depends more on which business you are in than on how well you row; switch boats rather than patch leaks.
principles.quote: a good managerial record (measured by economic returns) is far more a function of what business boat you get into than it is of how effectively you row

principles.text: Capital spending that looks rational for each company in a commodity industry is irrational collectively, because everyone's costs and prices fall together.
principles.quote: Viewed individually, each company’s capital investment decision appeared cost-effective and rational; viewed collectively, the decisions neutralized each other and were irrational

principles.text: Judge earnings growth by the additional capital it required; adding earnings by retaining and adding capital at ordinary returns is no great achievement.
principles.quote: When returns on capital are ordinary, an earn-more-by-putting-up-more record is no great managerial achievement.

principles.text: Fixed-price, ten-year options ignore capital costs and individual performance; option holders have no downside, unlike owners.
principles.quote: No owner has ever escaped the burden of capital costs, whereas a holder of a fixed-price option bears no capital costs at all.

principles.text: Growth eventually dampens exceptional economics: high-return companies cannot keep reinvesting all earnings at high rates once they are large.
principles.quote: an iron law of business is that growth eventually dampens exceptional economics.

principles.text: The key to successful investing is buying shares in good businesses when market prices are at a large discount from underlying business values.
principles.quote: we had learned from Ben Graham that the key to successful investing was the purchase of shares in good businesses when market prices were at a large discount from underlying business values.
